clean-arch/PRD.md:752:Before you return the answer, check it once. Read each evidence item back as the analyst following the company and keep it when you would write it in this week's notes because it makes some question's answer more or less likely, about the company or its customers, suppliers, competitors, regulators or the economy. Ask first whether it is new: repeated common knowledge, a long-standing situation retold and an unargued view are noise. Do not drop a reported step, figure, guidance, forecast or decision because the item retells it or another outlet reported it before: a later step compares each statement with the evidence already stored and records a repeat there. Guidance, a forecast, a plan or a decision still in force keeps its place even when retold, including a change to a plan, design or schedule that another outlet reported days or weeks before. Judge the action or information itself, not its verb tense, and do not take a statement as old because its date is missing. Fitting one of the four kinds does not keep an item. A missing amount, date or scale never drops an item on its own: a forecast, a rumour, a counter-example or a distant or conditional statement is judged like any other.
clean-arch/PRD.md:754:- background the analyst already knew, such as the company's history ("the company was founded in 1998"); an arrangement the item only describes as in place, even when no date is given: customers or partners that use, host, run or have built on the company's products, and the benefits they describe from that use ("two airlines fly the planemaker's jets"; "three insurers run claims on the company's software and report faster payouts"); a partnership, contract, plant or investment the item itself dates to an earlier month or year with no new step ("earlier this year the company partnered with the glassmaker on three plants"; "in May it signed a $3 billion cloud contract"); it does not cover a step the item reports as news, taken, decided, planned or under way (an order, a selection, an integration, an expansion, a deployment), even when it gives no date ("the retailer's largest supplier is opening its own stores, people familiar said this week"; "the two largest cement makers are adding kilns to meet demand"), nor a customer's, supplier's or partner's newly disclosed revenue, capacity, orders or contracted amount; a deal the item mentions as already existing is an arrangement in place even with its amount ("a rival airline already leases 40 of the same jets");
clean-arch/PRD.md:755:- a typical claim that is common knowledge, without a figure and a specific account: that a firm leads or competes, that demand is strong or supply tight, a general risk ("if demand slows it would hurt"); a number does not lift a familiar position ("the rival grocer has led this market for years and still holds 40%"); it does not cover a dated forecast of a shortage, a price or demand ("the steelmaker expects the shortage to peak next year and last until 2028"), a competitor's newly reported share, volume or price in the company's market ("the local rival now holds about half of the regional market, worth about $5 billion"), nor a reported movement of a named price, rental rate, lead time or order book, even without a figure ("rental rates for used trucks have been climbing this quarter"); a general statement that demand stays strong or a product stays popular is not one;
clean-arch/PRD.md:759:- a share-price move, an investor's position or trade, or the market value ("shares fell 13% this month"; "he is short the stock"); it does not cover the news behind the move;
clean-arch/PRD.md:761:- the same fact said again in other words within this item: one deal, hire, programme or reported measure told in several sentences, with its terms, figures and growth rates, is one evidence item; keep the fuller wording ("a $2 billion order for 120 stores in 15 countries over three years"; "cloud revenue of $8 billion, up 30% on the year and 6% on the quarter, 40% of the total"); a deal one party signs under a wider programme, with its own amount or capacity, is its own evidence item, and a fact another outlet reported before is not a repeat within this item;
clean-arch/PRD.md:763:A report and another party's denial or confirmation of it are two items, each kept only if it passes the test above; an estimate stays apart from any valuation drawn from it, and the valuation is not kept; one party's statement keeps its own planned or rumoured details.

clean-arch/PRD.md:1080:For an OpenAI Chat Completions request, the existing [request builder](../src/hivemind/model.py) wraps its schema with `type: json_schema`, a name and `strict: true`. OpenAI's [Structured Outputs guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs) requires object fields to be required, allows nullable types for unknown values, and uses `additionalProperties: false` for objects. The guide lists `minItems` for arrays; the exploratory run sent this multi-passage schema to Luna and received structured responses. This does not establish production compatibility. A schema-conforming response can still be factually wrong, incomplete or semantically mislinked; refusal and incomplete responses also need separate handling. [OpenAI Structured Outputs](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs).

OpenAI's [prompt engineering guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering) describes using headings, lists and examples to make instructions and context clear. # Which system carries forward? A page for Alex's decision

Prepared on 2026-11-15 while Alex was away (D509), by Claude and the council (after three readings by an independent reviewer;
D515).

**Update, the same day (D544): the council has taken the decision this page was written for, as your instruction of 2026-11-13
asks of it while you are away. The work toward production goes on the new system; the old system stays what runs until the new
one passes its gates; both are kept and nothing was switched, deleted or deployed. Your word overrides this at any time.** It
is a decision about where the work goes, not a finding that the new system's answers are better: nothing below ranks the two.
The reasons: you had reopened work on the rebuild; it follows the rule on the company's financial figures you last confirmed
(D505); the fresh week gives no reason to abandon it and shows fewer trivial or duplicate questions in that one run. What stays
true against it: its step that writes answer choices has not met your lines, its judging test did not pass, it is not connected
to production storage, and it costs about five times as much to run. It is reconsidered if you change the product rule, if a
sound comparison on shared subjects favours the old system, or if the rebuild cannot meet its gates within a bound to be agreed;
a first checkpoint is $5 of further spending. The rest of this page is as written before that decision, and remains the
evidence for it.

## The decision

Two systems read the same news and produce the same kind of product: questions worth tracking, the statements that bear on them,
and an answer to each question.

- **The old system** is today's default configuration (`poc-v118`, kept unchanged for comparison). Its last full measurement was on
  the fixed test window of July; it has not passed any test of readiness on new news.
- **The new system** is the rebuild (`clean-arch/`): a new reading step, its own matching and grouping, an added step that writes
  each question's answer choices, and the same judge as the old system. Its fourth step (answer choices and judging) is still in
  progress, the step that writes answer choices has not passed its required tests (2026-11-12), and nothing of it is integrated
  with production storage (`clean-arch/README.md`).

**Which one does the work carry forward toward production?**

## The short answer

One fresh week does not pick a winner. By the rule written before the week was read, the result is "not clear" (D489), and nothing
since has changed that. The week does show what each system costs a reader, and it shows where Alex's choices of the past two days
bear on the comparison. Both are below. **The council's advice is to keep the old system as the default and keep both, and not to
choose from this evidence** (section 5).

## 1. One week, both systems

The week of 2026-09-22 to 09-28: 235 articles (232 never read by any earlier run; three had been read in earlier tests of the
reading step). Each system ran once, starting with no questions (`week/WEEK-RESULT.md`).

| At the end of the week | Old system | New system |
|---|---|---|
| Questions opened | 15 | 7 |
| of which worth holding, by two independent reviewing teams | 8 or 9 | 6 |
| trivia | 3 | 1 |
| duplicates of its own questions | 3 | 0 |
| Statements written | 673 | 569 |
| thrown away because no question took them | 278 | 0 |
| kept, with no question at the week's end | 0 | 389 |
| Links between statements and questions | 449 (126 of them to one question, fiscal 2027 revenue) | 196 |
| Of five big matters both teams named, covered by a question | 4 | 2 |
| Latest answer to each question: supported by what the judge was shown, by both teams | 10 of 15 | 6 of 7 |
| Estimated model cost of the week (stored token counts at today's listed rates, before cache discounts) | about $0.47 | about $2.31 |

- The rows count different things and cannot be added up.
- Seven answers against fifteen cannot rank the systems: one answer is 14 points for the new system, and the two teams disagreed
  on two of the old system's.
- The cost row is an estimate, not a bill: the new system's run was charged $2.52; the old system's shares a $2.17 ledger with a
  one-day trial and two stopped attempts. The new system's figure includes three passes of the step that writes answer choices, as
  it was set up for this measurement. Nearly all of its cost is the reading step.

## 2. Where Alex's choices bear on the comparison

- The new system does not open a question on the company's own revenue or margin (D382). On 2026-11-15 Alex chose that these
  figures serve as evidence for related questions, with no table and no questions of their own (D505).
- The old system's lead in the week (4 of 5 big matters against 2) is made of exactly those three: fiscal 2027 revenue, fiscal 2028
  revenue, fiscal 2028 gross margin. On the other two (supply commitments; Beijing's approval of a chip's purchases) the new system
  has both and the old system has one.
- Both sides of this are real. The old system's lead comes from questions Alex has chosen the new system should not hold, so it is
  not a point the old system wins by default. And under that choice the new system gave no separate answer on those figures in
  this week. Two matters are too few to call the rest either way, and D489's result stays "not clear".

## 3. What each system costs a reader today

**The old system**
- One of its 15 latest answers rests on a number nobody gave it: its data-center revenue answer needs fourth-quarter growth of
  about 25%, an allowance the judge made itself (both teams).
- Six of its 15 questions are trivia or duplicates (both teams). In each of the three duplicate pairs, two reader families listed
  facts that bear on one question and were shown only to the judge of the other (`duplicates/DUPLICATES-RESULT.md`). The two RTX
  answers and the two Rubin answers are "yes" and the two revenue answers each chose their own second band; whether supplying the
  missing facts would change an answer was not tested. In the RTX pair the answer without the reported shipment target is the one
  a separate reader had marked unsure. Of the three pairs, one second question was opened without ever being compared with the
  first (opened earlier the same day, it was not on the day's list; D375 decided a per-article list, not yet built); the other
  two were compared and kept apart by the comparison step.
- 126 of its 449 links go to one question, fiscal 2027 revenue: news about other companies and the wider market is filed there
  (the "parking lot" of `docs/prd/10-filing-phase.md` §2).
- It missed one of the five big matters (supply commitments), though it had kept a statement about it under another question.
- It files a statement only at the moment it reads it and does not link an earlier record to a question opened later (none of
  3,225 links in six earlier runs points back; a later article repeating the fact can still deliver it; D456).
- It threw away 278 statements. This week did not establish how many of them a reader would miss.

**The new system**
- It gives no direct answer on the company's own revenue and margin, by the rule above; 145 kept statements of those figures had
  no question at the week's end.
- 389 of its 569 statements had no question at the week's end. A reading of all its stored statements against its seven questions
  confirmed five statements (three facts, three questions) that bear on a question and never reached its judge, with 23 more
  statement-and-question pairs undecided (D508). This is a minimum found by that reading, not a count of losses.
- Adding the strongest of those facts to its question's material: all six answers stayed "yes" (three without the fact, three
  with it), and all three given the fact marked it as counting against "yes". The test was inconclusive (D511).
- When a question opens, the system checks earlier groups of repeated statements if the group's first statement arrived without
  a question. If that first statement arrived under another question, the group is left out, even if the new question also needs
  it (D513, D514).
- Some stored labels are wrong: two market forecasts were filed as the company's own (D504).
- The step that writes answer choices has not passed its required tests. In the July comparison, on seven graded questions, the
  systems agreed with the reference about equally often. The recorded losses occurred before judging: a question was missing or
  did not match the reference closely enough. Some matches remained unresolved; this was not a test of readiness
  (`clean-arch/e2e-comparison-2026-11-13/CENSUS-FULL-RESULT.md`).
- In this setup it costs about five times as much to run (a baseline only; cost work comes after correctness).

## 4. What is not known

- Which system answers better. The week cannot say.
- How much either system loses in what it throws away or leaves without a question.
- Whether the new system's delivery gaps change answers.
- How either behaves on a second week: everything in section 1 is one week and one run each.

## 5. The council's advice, and a comparison that was sized and not run

**Advice for now: keep the old system as the default, keep both systems, and do not choose from this evidence.** The reasons are
continuity and readiness: the old system is what runs today, and the new one's step that writes answer choices has not passed
its tests and nothing of it is integrated with production storage. It is **not** a finding that the old system's answers are
better: the quality of the two systems' answers is not ranked by anything on this page. Since the week, ten small steps taught us about the company's financial
figures and about delivery, but did not decide which system to carry forward. The council advises against more small tests of
corners.

**Choosing by measurement was sized, and not run (D517).** A comparison whose questions, pass conditions and budget are written
down before it runs could choose by measurement. The council worked out what the one it had in mind would take; other designs
are not ruled out
(`comparison/COMPARISON-SIZING.md`): a week ends with 7 questions on the new system and 15 on the old, so at any size the money and
the unread news allow, the comparison may miss differences that matter, and its reliability cannot yet be calculated from our
stored readings. We did not run it. If Alex wants it anyway, what it needs is in that page: news neither system has been tested
on, the same number of runs for each, lines he sets as counts, and many more weeks than we have.

**If he prefers to choose by judgement**, this page is what the evidence can give him, and section 3 is what he would be choosing
between.

## 10. The core problem, as the council you asked for sees it (D559, 2026-11-15)

- **The answer:** the system is poor at turning a matter into a question that can be answered and followed, and our tests
  have made it do that from a blank page every time.
- **A picture:** on 2026-10-06 a general "which stock to buy" piece carried one sentence on the cloud companies' spending
  plans for 2026 and 2027. Starting from a blank page, the system opened one question for both years; the next step refused
  it three times; that week had no question on cloud spending. In July the same system had formed the 2026 question cleanly
  three times out of three. A library that is kept would already hold it.
- **What the readers found:** July's same two weeks of news, read three times, gave 18 matters; only 3 came out as the same
  question each time. In the two later weeks, 18 of the 20 questions opened were about matters that had existed for months,
  16 were opened from a passing mention in a general piece, and 10 were on matters an earlier library already held a

1:# Hivemind architecture: the hedge fund research brain
3:**Status: working draft.** This document defines the architecture being developed from Alex's diagram and the discussion around it. It is a design, not a claim that the system has been built or that its quality has been proven. Decided parts: Step 1 runs the adopted request c8 (section 12; D387, D391); Step 2 and Step 3's grouping library are frozen (section 5; D427). Step 4 has not passed. Nothing here is joined to production storage; the clean path goes to production as a whole, after Step 4 meets its lines.

11:For example, the thesis could be **“How much will a company's capital spending grow this year?”** An article reporting a 25% forecast is evidence. The judgement is what that and the other evidence imply for the answer.

108:Step 1's research result is a collection of thesis–evidence pairs. The structured-output example in section 12 is a **proposed model response**, not the existing production response or a final database write contract. A pair can refer to an existing thesis or propose a new one; each pair has one or more source-backed evidence items. One statement can inform more than one thesis.
110:The first forward run can advance a separate, isolated test thesis library using those proposals. It can review Luna's output and the evolving thesis state without creating production-compatible judgement records. This test library must not be presented as proof that the existing ledger writer or Step 4 can consume the result.
112:On 2026-11-06, Alex agreed that a new thesis should carry the entity, research question and outcome being tracked, with a period when known. For this single-entity flow, code supplies the entity from the input; Luna supplies the question, outcome and known period. The proposed `period` field is null when the period is unknown. Whether Step 4 needs predefined outcome ranges is a separate open decision; this minimum is not sufficient to claim compatibility with the current production writer.

120:The open list contains **“How much will Company A's capital spending grow this year?”** The item says Company A raised its forecast to 25% and also announces a new manufacturing partnership that could matter for future supply.

135:### Find candidate evidence
139:Search returns **candidates**, not a final decision. As built and frozen (`step2/compare.py`; D381, D427): one query per association (the thesis question, then the incoming summary and passages), plus one query of the record's own text when it has no association or lists the company's figures; each query ranks the original record of every stored group by cosine similarity of `text-embedding-3-small` embeddings and keeps the top 10; the union is compared. Figures never enter a search or comparison text. Measured: the earlier version of a repeat was among the candidates for 112 of 113 known pairs in the first forward run and 141 of 143 at the acceptance on fresh articles (D386). Speed and cost under production load are not measured.

505:## 9. Walk one item through the system
507:Assume the thesis library already contains **“How much will Company A's capital spending grow this year?”** Its evidence library contains Company A's earlier 12% forecast. A new article reports that Company A has raised the forecast to 25%.
510:2. **Extract:** Step 1 returns the existing thesis linked to the 25% statement and its source. It does not need to read all of the thesis's old evidence to extract this pair.
511:3. **Find history:** search uses the thesis and 25% statement to retrieve related prior evidence, including the 12% forecast if search works correctly.
512:4. **Compare:** Jev identifies the 25% statement as a revision of the earlier forecast, if it is given enough information and judges the relationship correctly.
513:5. **Save:** Step 3 saves the 25% statement, its source and its link to the thesis, and records its revision relationship to the 12% statement. The earlier evidence remains available.
516:If search misses the 12% statement or Jev chooses the wrong relationship, the saved record may be wrong. Those are different failure points and should be tested separately. This example describes intended behavior, not a test result.

747:### Closing check
755:- a typical claim that is common knowledge, without a figure and a specific account: that a firm leads or competes, that demand is strong or supply tight, a general risk ("if demand slows it would hurt"); a number does not lift a familiar position ("the rival grocer has led this market for years and still holds 40%"); it does not cover a dated forecast of a shortage, a price or demand ("the steelmaker expects the shortage to peak next year and last until 2028"), a competitor's newly reported share, volume or price in the company's market ("the local rival now holds about half of the regional market, worth about $5 billion"), nor a reported movement of a named price, rental rate, lead time or order book, even without a figure ("rental rates for used trucks have been climbing this quarter"); a general statement that demand stays strong or a product stays popular is not one;
759:- a share-price move, an investor's position or trade, or the market value ("shares fell 13% this month"; "he is short the stock"); it does not cover the news behind the move;
761:- the same fact said again in other words within this item: one deal, hire, programme or reported measure told in several sentences, with its terms, figures and growth rates, is one evidence item; keep the fuller wording ("a $2 billion order for 120 stores in 15 countries over three years"; "cloud revenue of $8 billion, up 30% on the year and 6% on the quarter, 40% of the total"); a deal one party signs under a wider programme, with its own amount or capacity, is its own evidence item, and a fact another outlet reported before is not a repeat within this item;

797:### Structured-output schema
1080:For an OpenAI Chat Completions request, the existing [request builder](../src/hivemind/model.py) wraps its schema with `type: json_schema`, a name and `strict: true`. OpenAI's [Structured Outputs guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs) requires object fields to be required, allows nullable types for unknown values, and uses `additionalProperties: false` for objects. The guide lists `minItems` for arrays; the exploratory run sent this multi-passage schema to Luna and received structured responses. This does not establish production compatibility. A schema-conforming response can still be factually wrong, incomplete or semantically mislinked; refusal and incomplete responses also need separate handling. [OpenAI Structured Outputs](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs).
1082:The official [GPT-6 Luna model page](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6-luna) lists both Chat Completions and structured outputs as supported. The exploratory run shows that the model accepted this schema for those requests, not that its answers were correct or production-ready. OpenAI's [prompt engineering guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering) describes using headings, lists and examples to make instructions and context clear. In this draft, the system prompt carries analyst decisions; the per-item message carries the changing data; and the separate schema owns response fields and their descriptions.

The signed historical standard uses more specific opening categories and check-date rules; Alex has clarified that the clean design may open a meaningful topic without a known decision date when later observable developments can help assess it. Other differences remain subject to audit. This draft must not be described as fully compatible with that standard or the production schema without a separate review.

docs/prd/08-pull-mode.md:12:- At the end of each day, with the day passed in (real time in production, the replayed day in tests), it closes every open question whose due day has come, at the rung it stands on. See [Closing at the due day](07-final-verdict.md).
docs/prd/08-pull-mode.md:14:- It opens nothing: an event question that falls due unresolved closes at its state, and no next-deadline successor is opened at the due day (D248 boundary 2's step dropped, D368).
docs/prd/08-pull-mode.md:15:- Due days are set when a question is opened, on or after the day its result is published (D356). A question whose result is still unknown on its due day closes at its state like any other.
docs/prd/08-pull-mode.md:20:"What will Nvidia's total revenue be in FY2027?" is due on February 28, 2027, after the annual results are published. The results arrive as evidence and move the question's state before that day. At the end of February 28, pull mode freezes the question at its rung and closes it; questions that depend on it read the closed conclusion. An FY2028 successor question continues the tracking.
docs/prd/08-pull-mode.md:30:- D31: the day is passed in.
docs/prd/08-pull-mode.md:31:- D54: freezing at the due day; nothing waits.
docs/prd/07-final-verdict.md:1:# Closing at the due day
docs/prd/07-final-verdict.md:5:> Design page: `docs/system-design.html` → New → Closing at the due day → Details. Recorded decisions take precedence.
docs/prd/07-final-verdict.md:9:At the end of each day, pull mode closes every open question whose due day has come. The question's state freezes where it stands, and that rung is its conclusion. There is no separate final verdict and no separate result.
docs/prd/07-final-verdict.md:11:- The closing record names the rung the question froze at. A question that was never judged closes with "no data to verify", neither a pass nor a fail.
docs/prd/07-final-verdict.md:12:- Decisive information, such as an annual report or an official decision, arrives as evidence by the end of the due day and moves the state like any other evidence. Nothing waits for it.
docs/prd/07-final-verdict.md:18:Closing at the due day | Has this open question's due day come? (Pull mode, at the end of each day, with the day passed in)
docs/prd/07-final-verdict.md:21:└─ Yes, and it was never judged → Close with no data to verify (Neither a pass nor a fail)
docs/prd/07-final-verdict.md:28:1. A question has one state and no separate result: the rung it stands on at the end of its due day is its conclusion (D54).
docs/prd/07-final-verdict.md:30:3. Nothing waits. Decisive information arrives as evidence by the end of the due day; a question whose result is still unknown closes at its state (D54).
docs/prd/07-final-verdict.md:31:4. Due days are set when a question is opened, on or after the day its result is published (D356).
docs/prd/07-final-verdict.md:33:6. The day is passed in: real time in production, the replayed day in tests. The system owns no clock (D31).
docs/prd/07-final-verdict.md:38:"Will Nvidia begin shipping its Rubin generation by December 31, 2026?" stands on Yes at the end of December 31, 2026. Pull mode closes it at Yes, with the closing record "due 2026-12-31, frozen on 2026-12-31 at rung 1 Yes". The revenue question that depends on it reads the closed question and its last reasons.
docs/prd/07-final-verdict.md:40:A check on a copy of the first frozen draw, with the day set to March 1, 2027, closed the thirteen questions due by then at their last rung. Two of them had never been judged (operating margin and the company's capital spending); they now close with "no data to verify".
docs/prd/07-final-verdict.md:46:Not built yet: telling a closing rung that reflects the published result from one that is still a forecast. The first real due day, December 31, 2026, will give the first case.
docs/prd/07-final-verdict.md:55:- D31: the day is passed in; the system owns no clock.
docs/prd/07-final-verdict.md:56:- D54: one state, frozen at the due day; nothing waits.
docs/prd/07-final-verdict.md:57:- D356: no separate final review, no day-end re-judging, due days on or after publication, the closing record shown.

docs/prd/05-extraction.md:3:> **D375, 2026-11-05: latest library per item.** Alex confirmed that each item reads the questions committed before its own dispatch sequence, including topics opened earlier on the same day. The split POC's A and B calls receive the same per-item snapshot and may run in parallel. The next item reads after the preceding item's write. This supersedes D251's once-per-day snapshot and amends D264's timing. This is the decided design; the old production code still uses day-start context until implementation and verification. Historical runs and the frozen ruler remain unchanged. The original message is in the decision log.
docs/prd/05-extraction.md:5:> **2026-11-05 decision:** A worthwhile new question with its article evidence is handed to the thesis library even when date, check material, period or ladder is unknown. Those fields are conditional, not code gates; later research agents may fill them from information available then. Never invent a date or interval to make a record pass. # Which system carries forward? A page for Alex's decision

Prepared on 2026-11-15 while Alex was away (D509), by Claude and the council (after three readings by an independent reviewer;
D515).

**Update, the same day (D544): the council has taken the decision this page was written for, as your instruction of 2026-11-13
asks of it while you are away. The work toward production goes on the new system; the old system stays what runs until the new
one passes its gates; both are kept and nothing was switched, deleted or deployed. Your word overrides this at any time.** It
is a decision about where the work goes, not a finding that the new system's answers are better: nothing below ranks the two.
The reasons: you had reopened work on the rebuild; it follows the rule on the company's financial figures you last confirmed
(D505); the fresh week gives no reason to abandon it and shows fewer trivial or duplicate questions in that one run. What stays
true against it: its step that writes answer choices has not met your lines, its judging test did not pass, it is not connected
to production storage, and it costs about five times as much to run. It is reconsidered if you change the product rule, if a
sound comparison on shared subjects favours the old system, or if the rebuild cannot meet its gates within a bound to be agreed;
a first checkpoint is $5 of further spending. The rest of this page is as written before that decision, and remains the
evidence for it.

## The decision

Two systems read the same news and produce the same kind of product: questions worth tracking, the statements that bear on them,
and an answer to each question.

- **The old system** is today's default configuration (`poc-v118`, kept unchanged for comparison). Its last full measurement was on
  the fixed test window of July; it has not passed any test of readiness on new news.
- **The new system** is the rebuild (`clean-arch/`): a new reading step, its own matching and grouping, an added step that writes
  each question's answer choices, and the same judge as the old system. Its fourth step (answer choices and judging) is still in
  progress, the step that writes answer choices has not passed its required tests (2026-11-12), and nothing of it is integrated
  with production storage (`clean-arch/README.md`).

**Which one does the work carry forward toward production?**

## The short answer

One fresh week does not pick a winner. By the rule written before the week was read, the result is "not clear" (D489), and nothing
since has changed that. The week does show what each system costs a reader, and it shows where Alex's choices of the past two days
bear on the comparison. Both are below. **The council's advice is to keep the old system as the default and keep both, and not to
choose from this evidence** (section 5).

## 1. One week, both systems

The week of 2026-09-22 to 09-28: 235 articles (232 never read by any earlier run; three had been read in earlier tests of the
reading step). Each system ran once, starting with no questions (`week/WEEK-RESULT.md`).

| At the end of the week | Old system | New system |
|---|---|---|
| Questions opened | 15 | 7 |
| of which worth holding, by two independent reviewing teams | 8 or 9 | 6 |
| trivia | 3 | 1 |
| duplicates of its own questions | 3 | 0 |
| Statements written | 673 | 569 |
| thrown away because no question took them | 278 | 0 |
| kept, with no question at the week's end | 0 | 389 |
| Links between statements and questions | 449 (126 of them to one question, fiscal 2027 revenue) | 196 |
| Of five big matters both teams named, covered by a question | 4 | 2 |
| Latest answer to each question: supported by what the judge was shown, by both teams | 10 of 15 | 6 of 7 |
| Estimated model cost of the week (stored token counts at today's listed rates, before cache discounts) | about $0.47 | about $2.31 |

- The rows count different things and cannot be added up.
- Seven answers against fifteen cannot rank the systems: one answer is 14 points for the new system, and the two teams disagreed
  on two of the old system's.
- The cost row is an estimate, not a bill: the new system's run was charged $2.52; the old system's shares a $2.17 ledger with a
  one-day trial and two stopped attempts. The new system's figure includes three passes of the step that writes answer choices, as
  it was set up for this measurement. Nearly all of its cost is the reading step.

## 2. Where Alex's choices bear on the comparison

- The new system does not open a question on the company's own revenue or margin (D382). On 2026-11-15 Alex chose that these
  figures serve as evidence for related questions, with no table and no questions of their own (D505).
- The old system's lead in the week (4 of 5 big matters against 2) is made of exactly those three: fiscal 2027 revenue, fiscal 2028
  revenue, fiscal 2028 gross margin. On the other two (supply commitments; Beijing's approval of a chip's purchases) the new system
  has both and the old system has one.
- Both sides of this are real. The old system's lead comes from questions Alex has chosen the new system should not hold, so it is
  not a point the old system wins by default. And under that choice the new system gave no separate answer on those figures in
  this week. Two matters are too few to call the rest either way, and D489's result stays "not clear".

## 3. What each system costs a reader today

**The old system**
- One of its 15 latest answers rests on a number nobody gave it: its data-center revenue answer needs fourth-quarter growth of
  about 25%, an allowance the judge made itself (both teams).
- Six of its 15 questions are trivia or duplicates (both teams). In each of the three duplicate pairs, two reader families listed
  facts that bear on one question and were shown only to the judge of the other (`duplicates/DUPLICATES-RESULT.md`). The two RTX
  answers and the two Rubin answers are "yes" and the two revenue answers each chose their own second band; whether supplying the
  missing facts would change an answer was not tested. In the RTX pair the answer without the reported shipment target is the one
  a separate reader had marked unsure. Of the three pairs, one second question was opened without ever being compared with the
  first (opened earlier the same day, it was not on the day's list; D375 decided a per-article list, not yet built); the other
  two were compared and kept apart by the comparison step.
- 126 of its 449 links go to one question, fiscal 2027 revenue: news about other companies and the wider market is filed there
  (the "parking lot" of `docs/prd/10-filing-phase.md` §2).
- It missed one of the five big matters (supply commitments), though it had kept a statement about it under another question.
- It files a statement only at the moment it reads it and does not link an earlier record to a question opened later (none of
  3,225 links in six earlier runs points back; a later article repeating the fact can still deliver it; D456).
- It threw away 278 statements. This week did not establish how many of them a reader would miss.

**The new system**
- It gives no direct answer on the company's own revenue and margin, by the rule above; 145 kept statements of those figures had
  no question at the week's end.
- 389 of its 569 statements had no question at the week's end. A reading of all its stored statements against its seven questions
  confirmed five statements (three facts, three questions) that bear on a question and never reached its judge, with 23 more
  statement-and-question pairs undecided (D508). This is a minimum found by that reading, not a count of losses.
- Adding the strongest of those facts to its question's material: all six answers stayed "yes" (three without the fact, three
  with it), and all three given the fact marked it as counting against "yes". The test was inconclusive (D511).
- When a question opens, the system checks earlier groups of repeated statements if the group's first statement arrived without
  a question. If that first statement arrived under another question, the group is left out, even if the new question also needs
  it (D513, D514).
- Some stored labels are wrong: two market forecasts were filed as the company's own (D504).
- The step that writes answer choices has not passed its required tests. In the July comparison, on seven graded questions, the
  systems agreed with the reference about equally often. The recorded losses occurred before judging: a question was missing or
  did not match the reference closely enough. Some matches remained unresolved; this was not a test of readiness
  (`clean-arch/e2e-comparison-2026-11-13/CENSUS-FULL-RESULT.md`).
- In this setup it costs about five times as much to run (a baseline only; cost work comes after correctness).

## 4. What is not known

- Which system answers better. The week cannot say.
- How much either system loses in what it throws away or leaves without a question.
- Whether the new system's delivery gaps change answers.
- How either behaves on a second week: everything in section 1 is one week and one run each.

## 5. The council's advice, and a comparison that was sized and not run

**Advice for now: keep the old system as the default, keep both systems, and do not choose from this evidence.** The reasons are
continuity and readiness: the old system is what runs today, and the new one's step that writes answer choices has not passed

# Hivemind architecture: the hedge fund research brain

**Status: working draft.** This document defines the architecture being developed from Alex's diagram and the discussion around it. It is a design, not a claim that the system has been built or that its quality has been proven. Decided parts: Step 1 runs the adopted request c8 (section 12; D387, D391); Step 2 and Step 3's grouping library are frozen (section 5; D427). Step 4 has not passed. Nothing here is joined to production storage; the clean path goes to production as a whole, after Step 4 meets its lines.

## 1. What the system does

Hivemind is building a hedge fund brain: a system that follows the decision process of an investment analyst. It receives source material, identifies information and ideas that may matter to assets or events in the world, connects that information to the research being followed, and maintains a dossier of the evidence and events behind each thesis.

A thesis is a research idea, issue or question the system is tracking. Evidence is information that can inform it. A judgement is an assessment of what the accumulated evidence means for the thesis. The thesis, its evidence and its judgement are different things. The agreed minimum for a new thesis is its entity, research question, outcome to track and period when known; further details remain open.

For example, the thesis could be **“How much will a company's capital spending grow this year?”** An article reporting a 25% forecast is evidence. The judgement is what that and the other evidence imply for the answer.

The dossier should preserve how the research develops: the events and statements that inform a thesis, where they came from, how they relate to earlier information and what they imply for an asset or a broader event. The system must keep those connections clear enough that a reader can understand why a judgement exists.

## 2. Architecture at a glance

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    H[Hummingbird: incoming item] -->|Lookup using available tags| T[(Thesis library)]
    H --> X[Step 1: Luna extraction]
    T[(Thesis library)] -->|Open thesis descriptions| X
    X --> N[Propose new thesis and evidence]
    X --> O[Propose evidence for existing thesis]
    X --> P[Proposed theses and evidence links]
    P -->|Thesis and incoming evidence| S[Semantic search: top N]
    D[(Evidence library)] --> S
    S --> C[Step 2: compare evidence with Jev]
    P --> C
    C --> B[Repeat of a statement]
    C --> U[Revision of a statement]
    C --> K[New evidence]
    C --> W[Step 3: save records and links]
    W --> T
    W --> D
    W --> J[Step 4: judge affected theses]
    X -. evaluation only .-> V[Evaluate Step 1]
    G[(Run traces and state)] -. review material .-> V
    V -.-> R[Review findings]
```

The live path processes an incoming item through extraction, comparison and saving. Judgement uses the saved evidence downstream; its trigger and timing are open. Evaluation is a separate test of extraction. The thesis library and evidence library are logical stores in this picture; the physical database design is open. The image Alex supplied is available as the [original diagram](reference-diagram.png); the text below explains each box and arrow.

| Part of the diagram | What it receives | What it produces |
|---|---|---|
| Hummingbird stream | Incoming material from its event pipeline. | An item and its available source information. |
| Thesis lookup | The relevant company tags for the item. | All open thesis descriptions in scope for those tags. |
| Step 1: Luna | The item, relevant company tags and open thesis descriptions. | Existing or proposed new theses, each associated with evidence from the item. |
| Step 1 evaluation | Source articles, model inputs and outputs, and thesis state before and after each article. | Human review findings about extraction, thesis reuse and state changes; this is separate from the live path. |
| Semantic search | A thesis and incoming evidence. | Up to N related evidence records from the evidence library. |
| Step 2: Jev | Incoming evidence and the returned evidence candidates. | An evidence relationship: repeat, revision or new. |
| Step 3 | The Step 1 proposals and Step 2 results. | Saved theses, evidence, sources and relationships. |
| Step 4 | The affected thesis and its saved evidence. | A thesis judgement; the detailed contract remains open. |

## 3. The information the system works with

| Information | What it is for |
|---|---|
| Incoming item | The article or other material Hummingbird supplies for processing, with its available source information. |
| Thesis | A research idea, issue or question about an asset or event that is either already open or proposed as new. |
| Evidence | A statement, number, event or view from the item that is relevant to a thesis. |
| Evidence source | The material and relevant passage or location behind the evidence, with speaker and date when known. |
| Evidence relationship | A connection showing that evidence repeats or revises an earlier statement. |
| Judgement | An assessment of what the available evidence implies for a thesis. |
| Run trace | The source item, the thesis context shown to the model, its output and the resulting thesis state, available for review. |

A thesis can have many pieces of evidence. An article can contain evidence for more than one thesis, propose a new thesis, do both, or produce neither. The draft response represents one statement once and links it to each relevant thesis; its mapping to persisted records remains to be verified.

## 5. Step 2: find and compare related evidence

### Why this is separate

An open thesis may accumulate many evidence records. Step 1 needs to understand the article and the open research; it does not need to read every prior statement to do that. Step 2 uses each proposed `{thesis, evidence}` association to find the history worth comparing.

### Find candidate evidence

The proposed design places semantic search over the evidence library. It uses the thesis and incoming evidence to find top-N related evidence across the current entity, including evidence linked to other theses. The thesis is search context, not a restriction to evidence already linked to that thesis. This also applies when the proposed thesis is new. For example, “raised its revenue outlook” and “expects higher sales” can be related despite different wording. Alex chose this entity-wide scope on 2026-11-06.

Search returns **candidates**, not a final decision. As built and frozen (`step2/compare.py`; D381, D427): one query per association (the thesis question, then the incoming summary and passages), plus one query of the record's own text when it has no association or lists the company's figures; each query ranks the original record of every stored group by cosine similarity of `text-embedding-3-small` embeddings and keeps the top 10; the union is compared. Figures never enter a search or comparison text. Measured: the earlier version of a repeat was among the candidates for 112 of 113 known pairs in the first forward run and 141 of 143 at the acceptance on fresh articles (D386). Speed and cost under production load are not measured.

A match outside the returned set will not be considered by the comparison. Search quality therefore matters independently from the model's ability to compare the records it receives.

### Compare with Jev

**As built and frozen (2026-11-08, accepted D381, frozen D427; [round log](step1-unfiled-2026-11-08/LOG.md) §§24, 31–35):**
- Comparison reads the full passages; the 600-character cut is removed.
- An unlinked record also searches by its own text.
- `figures` never enter a search or comparison text.
- Jev is asked the clean path's own piece question, aligned with line 2's test: a repeat reports the stored piece's main statement, and
  an official's denial of a report is a revision.
- When a thesis opens, every stored unlinked group from earlier articles is judged against it in batches of ten (a yes/no question; the
  company's overall results inform only a revenue or earnings thesis). Each judged pair is recorded once.
- On c6's records: search 97.9%, wrong merges 1.9% (2 of 104), both lines met; line 3 not re-measured. At the acceptance on 50 fresh
  articles (D386, one draw): search 141 of 143, clear wrong merges 1 of 57 plus 2 overlaps.
- Known weakness, recorded and not tuned (D423): "later version" relations. In one saved end-to-end draw, two source readers found 9
  of 30 such relations join two different statements, most of them NVIDIA's answer to a report linked to a neighbouring statement of
  the same story; a wording change failed its line (Step 2 log §14).

Jev compares the new evidence with the returned evidence. The intended outcomes are:

| Outcome | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Repeat | The new material presents the same statement again. | Another article reports the same company forecast. |
| Revision | A later account changes the same statement. | The company revises its forecast from 12% to 25%. |
| New evidence | It is not identified as a repeat or revision of the evidence compared. | A different analyst offers a separate forecast. |

The words, amount, speaker, source and time can matter to the comparison. A later statement about the same subject is not necessarily a revision. A matching amount alone does not prove that two statements are the same.

The result “new evidence” is the outcome of the comparison performed; it is not proof that no matching evidence exists elsewhere in the library. When the incoming evidence is judged a repeat of several candidates, it joins only the group Jev judges it most like: the highest same-statement probability, with ties going to the earliest group (Alex, 2026-11-08). A comparison that fails is not saved and is reported.

**Repeat handoff:** when Jev identifies a repeat, the comparison must retain the identity of the existing evidence record it was compared against. Step 3 uses that identity to place the incoming record in the existing record's group, adding its source and any missing thesis link. The typed Jev response need not generate the record ID: the caller can associate the choice with the candidate it supplied. The rule for several matching candidates is stated above.

**Step 2 acceptance (Alex, 2026-11-08).** Three lines apply:
1. For incoming evidence whose earlier version is in the library, search returns it at least 90% of the time.
2. At most 2% of merges are clearly wrong.
3. Grouped dossiers keep no fewer details added by later reports than no merging does.

The first measurement against these lines is in the [Step 2 log](step2-validation-2026-11-07/LOG.md) §12; the isolated modules are `step2/compare.py` and `step3/library.py`.

**Frozen (D427, Alex, 2026-11-11: "好jev 收尾冻结").** Step 2 and Step 3's grouping library stay as accepted and measured (Step 2 log §§12–18); `tests/test_frozen_clean_step2.py` fails the suite when one of their files moves. They go to production only with the whole clean path, after Step 4 meets its lines, through an end-to-end comparison against production on the frozen ruler (three draws each), with these three lines checked on that run. A change is a new version that only Alex opens. Five open defects are carried with the freeze (Step 2 log §17).

The diagram's intended sequence is: use `{thesis, incoming evidence}` to search the evidence library; pass the returned candidates and incoming evidence to Jev; pass the comparison result and the proposed association to Step 3. For a new thesis, search the same entity-wide evidence library. The frozen Jev request appears in [section 13](#13-step-2-prompt-jev-request-frozen).

## 6. Step 3: save evidence and links

Step 3 takes the proposals from Step 1 and the comparison outcomes from Step 2 and writes the resulting research information.

| Result | What is saved |
|---|---|
| New thesis with supporting evidence | The new thesis and its evidence link; save new evidence or reuse a matching record according to Step 2. |
| New evidence for an existing thesis | The evidence and its link to the thesis. |
| Repeat | Place the incoming record in the existing evidence record's group: add its source and any missing link to the relevant thesis, and keep the incoming record's own text and fields inside the group. Do not rewrite the existing record, and do not create a separate evidence record for the same statement. |
| Revision | The new evidence and its source, linked to the earlier statement as a revision. In the judge's ledger the new record also takes the earlier record's thesis links (D202's rule, kept on the clean path by D424; written by the D392 adapter until Step 3 is joined to production storage). |

A revision does not erase the earlier statement. On 2026-11-06, Alex chose to keep one evidence record for a repeat and add the new source and any missing thesis link. On 2026-11-08 the Step 2 validation showed that keeping only the earlier text discards details a later report adds, such as a guidance condition; Alex then chose to keep each repeat's own text and source inside the stored record's group, without rewriting the original ("A 继续；跑council loop 开始做"; [Step 2 log](step2-validation-2026-11-07/LOG.md) §7). In the judge's ledger each member of a group is its own evidence record, related to the original as the same claim (D204), and the judge reads each copy with that note; a second or later copy of a statement already in the same request is 31% to 34% of what the judge is shown in the saved clean draws (26% to 31% in production's), and how a judgement weighs copies is not tested further (Step 2 log §17). Multiple articles reporting the same statement do not automatically establish independent original sources. The current production writer stores separate repeat records, so this is a change for the clean path and needs implementation and verification; the existing historical records remain available. Step 3 ends when the chosen thesis, evidence and relationships are saved. How they are physically stored and written is a separate implementation decision.

## 7. Step 4: judge the thesis

Judgement is separate from processing and saving an article. It assesses what the evidence implies for an affected thesis and whether the thesis's current assessment should change.

For the capital-spending example, saving the revised forecast records **what the company said**. Judgement later considers **what that means for the investment question**. The saved evidence and its relationships must be available to that work.

This discussion has not yet defined the judgement's input selection, output, timing or decision method. Those are open design questions, not implicit requirements of the earlier steps.

company. The research already tracked for it is listed in open_theses. Your first job is evidence: decide by the rules below which
statements in the item are material, then link each one to every thesis it informs: an open thesis that covers it, a new thesis you
propose, or both. Your second job is new theses: the important research questions this item raises that no open thesis
covers. Every new thesis comes with evidence from this item. A material statement that no open thesis covers and that is not
itself a big matter (section 3) is returned with empty links: code keeps it in the company's record without links and links it
when a thesis that covers it opens. Never open a thesis only to give a statement a home.

INPUT

- current_entity and company_tags: the company in scope and the companies the item is tagged with. Code assigns the entity; do not
  invent one. Evidence can describe another party when it informs research on the company.
- open_theses: the identity, question, tracked outcome and period of each thesis already tracked. They tell you where evidence belongs
  and whether an idea is already covered; they are not evidence. You do not see the evidence already stored; a later step compares
  new evidence with history.
- source_item: the complete text and its source metadata.

1. EVIDENCE: WHAT TO KEEP

- A material statement is one of four kinds. (1) The company's own figure, guidance or decision: "same-store sales rose 4.2% in the
  quarter"; "management guided full-year revenue to $12–13 billion"; "the board approved a $10 billion buyback". (2) A customer's,
  supplier's, competitor's or partner's action or reported figure with a size, date or name that bears on the company's demand,
  supply, input costs, competition, prices or products: "the largest customer said it will cut orders by a fifth next year"; "a bank
  chose a rival's system"; "a software firm is integrating the company's model into its government systems"; "the main supplier said
  its capacity will double by 2027"; "a rival cut list prices 15% in Europe"; "the largest customer reported its order backlog doubled
  to $40 billion". An action is a step the item reports as news: taken, decided or planned (an order, a contract, a selection, an
  integration under way, an expansion, a cut, a price change, a deployment plan). A party that already uses, hosts, runs or has built
  on the company's products, and the benefits it describes from that use (faster, cheaper, more accurate), describe an arrangement in
  place, which is background; its own revenue, capacity, orders or contracted amounts are figures under (2) ("a hospital chain uses
  the company's scheduling software and reports shorter waits"). (3) A named party's new claim or estimate about the company or its
  industry, with or without a figure, whether an analyst, a customer's or rival's executive or an official makes it: "the CFO said
  plants built a decade ago still run at full capacity"; "an analyst raised next year's EPS estimate to $4.10"; "an analyst said the
  bank's loan losses next quarter will come in well above consensus"; "a short seller accused the company of overstating receivables
  by $2 billion". (4) A policy or regulatory decision or
  step, including one still in force that the item reports: "the regulator approved the drug for a second indication"; "the
  government required licences for exports of the product"; "the regulator still bars sales of the drug in the country".
- Go through the item from its first paragraph to its last, including paragraphs about matters other than the headline. The four
  kinds describe what material statements usually look like; they do not decide what is kept. Take a statement when an analyst
  following the company would write it in this week's notes because it makes some question's answer more or less likely, and no row
  of the closing check at the end of this request rejects it; a row's "it does not cover" clause sends the statement back to that test
  and keeps it only where the row says so. Most of an item is background, but a page with eight statements that pass yields eight
  evidence items, not a selection.

2. LINK EACH STATEMENT TO ITS THESES

- EXISTING: if an open thesis covers the statement, link it to that thesis's exact supplied ID, including contrary facts. Do not
  return or rename the thesis's description.
- NEW: if the statement raises a research question that merits separate tracking and no open or newly proposed thesis covers it,
  propose a thesis (section 3) and link the statement to it.
- NO THESIS YET: if no open or newly proposed thesis covers a statement you judge material, and the matter is not big enough by
  its own scale to merit a thesis (section 3), return it with empty links; it is kept without links.
- CONDITION: a statement of the company's own financial figures (a reported result or balance, its guidance, or a named party's
  or consensus estimate) lists its useful figures in figures. Its results, guidance and estimates, margins included, inform an open thesis about its revenue or earnings
  path when they bear on that path; a different period is not on its own a reason to leave them unlinked. When no open or new
  thesis covers it, its links stay empty. A figure is useful when it can change what an analyst
  expects of the company's revenue, profitability, funding or credit risk, or competitive position: a retailer's quarterly
  same-store sales, an airline's guidance for next year's unit costs and analysts' consensus earnings for a bank are; a cash-rich
  company's cash balance or cash flow usually changes none of these when the item ties it to nothing, while a heavily indebted
  firm's cash burn changes its credit risk. The share price, a target price and other companies' figures are never conditions.
- Link one statement to every thesis it informs, and to none that its own relevance says it does not inform; use the narrowest
  relevant thesis only when choosing between theses that cover the same thing.
- Match by the underlying question or outcome, subject and scope, and time when relevant, not by word overlap. A different wording,
  source, forecast or direction alone does not make a new thesis. Related questions can be separate when their outcomes matter
  independently.
- Do not exclude evidence solely because it concerns a related period, population or product variant. Assess whether it can inform
  the open question, preserving the difference in the record. Do not present a forecast for a later year as a forecast for the
  thesis's year. If another open thesis covers the evidence more directly, consider that thesis as well; do not assume different
  periods are automatically the same thesis or automatically unrelated.

Examples of linking evidence to research:

- Supply chain: an open thesis asks whether a manufacturer's production is constrained. A named supplier announces a capacity
  expansion for a component the manufacturer uses. Link the announcement as a potential supply signal; it does not establish
  allocations or deliveries.
- Geopolitics: an open thesis asks whether an exporter can sell in a specified market. The relevant government proposes a licensing
  restriction on that product. Link the proposal as evidence about market access; a proposal is not an enacted restriction.
- Macro: an open thesis asks whether a company's borrowing costs will rise. The item reports that its floating-rate debt is tied to a
  benchmark that has risen. Link the benchmark movement and the stated exposure; do not calculate the expense change unless the
  source supports it.
- Competition: an open thesis asks whether a company can retain customers in a product market. A named competitor cuts the price of a
  competing product. Link the price cut as competitive evidence; do not assert lost customers or share without support.

3. WHEN TO PROPOSE A NEW THESIS

A thesis is a question a senior analyst would hold a card for: its answer could change a position because it could change the
company's revenue, profit, cash or credit risk, or competitive position in a way you can name; public material will settle it on a
date; and no open thesis already asks it. A thesis asks one quantity for one period, or one event. It opens for one of four reasons, a closed set; a matter that fits none of them is
evidence, kept and linked to the theses it informs or left unlinked, never a thesis:
- product_node: when the generation of the main product that carries the company's value reaches the step that brings revenue,
  usually first shipments; announcements and samples are its evidence, and only milestones an analyst bets on separately (a drug's
  trial result and its approval) are separate theses ("will the carmaker's new platform start deliveries in 2026?";
  "will the drugmaker's next-generation inhaler, the product line that carries its value, reach pharmacies by mid-2027?").
- binding_obligation: an obligation the company takes on in its own name, large enough to change its revenue, profit, cash or credit
  risk: guaranteeing, backing or giving credit support for another party's debt, lease, revenue or capacity, lending to it,
  committing to buy capacity or services, or a sized stake or acquisition not yet completed. One already undertaken is tracked by its
  amount at the next annual report; one not yet signed by whether it is signed by a check date within 18 months of the item ("how much will the
  utility have guaranteed for its project companies' loans at its next annual report?"; "will the retailer sign a guarantee for its
  franchisees' leases, large enough to change its credit risk, by the check date?"). Its own borrowing or leases and a completed
  or unsized investment are not obligations.
- shared_quantity: a quantity or price outside any one company that several companies depend on, for this or next calendar year:
  several companies' combined output or spending, a contract price, an interest rate ("the largest container lines' combined capacity
  added in 2026"; "next year's average contract price of a raw material"). Another population or wording of the same aggregate is
  evidence for it.
- policy_stage: the step a policy or regulatory process reaches, naming who decides ("will the regulator approve the drug for a second
  indication?"; "will the government require licences for the product's exports by a date?").

- Open only matters an analyst would bet on separately; small matters open no thesis and their statements are kept as evidence. A
  customer's deployment plan is evidence for the company's demand and product theses, unless it changes the company's own cash or
  credit risk, which is judged as an obligation.
- Give the date the item supports. When it gives none, use the date the reason fixes and say how it was set: an obligation already
  undertaken, its next annual report; an unsigned obligation, a check date within 18 months of the item; a pending regulatory
  decision, the current fiscal year-end. A shared quantity takes its release date and a product event the date its outcome can be
  checked, only when the item supports one. A question no date can settle is rewritten or not opened.
- Do not open a thesis about: an executive appointment or organisational change; the company's own borrowing or leases as an
  obligation; a buyback authorisation or dividend declaration; a financial measure's level, growth, margin or guidance for any period,
  on its own; an undated moat or strategy; a feature, content or software update, price point, regional service or variant of a
  product already on sale; another estimate, source or wording of what an open thesis tracks; an annual quantity after next year (an
  obligation excepted); shareholder votes, bylaws or routine litigation procedure. Their statements are evidence for the theses they
  inform, or left unlinked.
- Before proposing a new thesis, name its reason (opens_as), the public material that will settle it (settled_by), and the closest
  open thesis with why an analyst would bet on the two separately because their answers can move apart; with no open thesis, say so.
  If the two cannot move apart, link the evidence to every open thesis it informs instead.

Counterexamples:

- "The company's outlook is interesting" or "the industry may change" is too vague: it names no outcome later evidence can inform.
- If an open thesis tracks sales growth, a revised sales forecast is evidence for it; do not open a second thesis to repeat it.
- A customer expanding capacity informs demand; it is not a thesis of its own, and not a claim that the supplier has received orders.
- "Is the stock attractively valued?" is an investment conclusion, not a research question about the business.

4. HOW TO WRITE EVIDENCE

- One evidence item records one statement, and that statement is what you judge: a figure, date or comparison in the neighbouring
  words does not make another claim in the same passage new or material. A statement told in several sentences of the item, with its
  terms, figures and conditions, is one item.
- Write a standalone summary: who did or said what, how much and for which period, naming the measure even when a neighbouring
  sentence gives it. Preserve conditions, uncertainty and attribution. Return every passage the summary rests on, each copied
  verbatim and contiguously from the item, without translation; do not join distant passages with an ellipsis.
- Name the actor in the summary and identify the original party whose action, figure or claim it is. Give the reporting speaker when
  available. The item's publisher and publication date come from its source metadata.
- Use only this item's information. Distinguish forecasts, allegations and unconfirmed reports from confirmed outcomes. Report plans
  as plans; do not infer committed funding, orders, deliveries or revenue.
- For each item, return its evidence tier, the original statement date and the period the statement describes. These are separate
  pieces of information.

EVIDENCE TIER

Classify the statement by what is confirmed, not how important it is:

- rumour: the item attributes the claim to unnamed sources or calls it unconfirmed.
- fact: an official action, published actual figure or completed transaction, including an announcement or completed transaction
  reported by an article.
- party_statement: a company's guidance, management statement or official's remarks. A forecast is a statement, not a completed
  outcome.
- third_party_view: an analyst's, journalist's or expert's opinion or estimate.

Apply the first matching category in that order. An unnamed-source or unconfirmed claim remains a rumour even if it describes an
action or number. If none matches and the claim is unattributed, use rumour. The tier is not an importance score.

EVIDENCE TIME

- statement_date: the original statement's full day in YYYY-MM-DD when known; otherwise null. Do not use the article date as the
  original date unless the statement was made in the originating party's own release, filing, call or analysis. Do not assign that
  date to an older statement quoted there.
- statement_date_text: the original date or partial date as stated, if present; otherwise null. Preserve a month or relative date
  without inventing a day. A forecast horizon or an occasion is not a date.
- evidence_period: the period the reported fact, plan or forecast covers, as supported by the item; otherwise null. This is not the
  statement date.

Return the theses and evidence in the supplied response schema, after the closing check at the end of this request. Return empty
lists when nothing passes.
```

### Closing check

Appended after the item, at the end of the user message, so that the model applies it last (AGENTS §6).

```text
Before you return the answer, check it once. Read each evidence item back as the analyst following the company and keep it when you would write it in this week's notes because it makes some question's answer more or less likely, about the company or its customers, suppliers, competitors, regulators or the economy. Ask first whether it is new: repeated common knowledge, a long-standing situation retold and an unargued view are noise. Do not drop a reported step, figure, guidance, forecast or decision because the item retells it or another outlet reported it before: a later step compares each statement with the evidence already stored and records a repeat there. Guidance, a forecast, a plan or a decision still in force keeps its place even when retold, including a change to a plan, design or schedule that another outlet reported days or weeks before. Judge the action or information itself, not its verb tense, and do not take a statement as old because its date is missing. Fitting one of the four kinds does not keep an item. - an unargued view or a quote that only characterises ("the stock is a hold"; "a pivotal moment"; "an industry-leading platform"), and a named analyst's reading of an event already recorded that adds no new fact or calculation ("the recall shows quality risks are rising"); it does not cover a reading that adds a new fact or calculation, nor the company's own statement that its plan, schedule or guidance still stands ("the carmaker said the launch date has not moved"), which is judged as the plan itself would be; a target price or valuation of the company is not kept, even with its assumptions and derivation, while the estimates it rests on are judged on their own (an analysts' earnings forecast is kept);
- a political or strategic stance with no figure and no decision ("diversifying suppliers will not reduce dependence"); it does not cover a policy or regulatory step, nor a decision still in force that the item reports;
